content: In 2015 and 2016, the WHO regional offices will organize a series of regional events to disseminate updated recommendations on contraceptive eligibility criteria. Additionally, special panel sessions will be held during the summer and autumn of 2015 at international conferences hosted by organizations such as the International Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (FIGO), the International Council of Nurses (ICN), and the International Confederation of Midwives (ICM). These sessions aim to inform members of these professional societies about the revised guidelines. Once translations of the updated document into other official UN languages are available, efforts will be made to ensure effective dissemination of the information. An evaluation survey will be conducted targeting ministries of health, WHO offices, partners, professional organizations, and civil society. This survey will assess the extent and effectiveness of the dissemination, evaluate the implementation of the guidance into national policies, and identify areas for further refinement and research gaps in contraceptive eligibility criteria. Regarding combined hormonal contraceptives (CHCs), the following questions were addressed: 1. Fracture Risk: Are women who use CHCs at an increased risk of fractures compared to non-users? Evidence from randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies was reviewed. The population studied included women of reproductive age. The intervention was CHC use, and the comparator was non-use of CHCs. The outcome measured was fracture risk. Databases searched included PubMed and the Cochrane Library. Evidence on this question is inconsistent, with some studies showing no effect of CHC use on fracture risk. 2. Bone Mineral Density (BMD): Are women, particularly adolescents, who use CHCs at an increased risk of decreased BMD compared to non-users? Evidence from randomized controlled trials, cohort studies, and case-control studies was reviewed. The population studied included women of reproductive age, with a specific focus on adolescents. The intervention was CHC use, and the comparator was non-use of CHCs. The outcome measured was decreased BMD. Databases searched included PubMed and the Cochrane Library. Evidence suggests that CHC use may decrease BMD in adolescents, especially with very-low-dose formulations (<30 µg ethinylestradiol). However, CHC use has little to no effect on BMD in premenopausal women and may preserve bone mass in perimenopausal women. Recommendations: Women from menarche to under 40 years of age can use CHCs (e.g., combined oral contraceptives, combined contraceptive patch, combined vaginal ring, combined injectable contraceptives) without restriction (MEC Category 1). Women aged 40 years and older can generally use CHCs (MEC Category 2). Remarks: In 2014, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) reviewed evidence on fracture risk among women of all ages and the potential for CHCs to decrease BMD in adolescents. BMD is a surrogate marker for fracture risk, but it may not accurately predict current or future fracture risk in premenopausal women. The risk of cardiovascular disease increases with age and may also increase with CHC use. In the absence of other adverse clinical conditions, CHCs can be used until menopause. Due to heterogeneity in study designs, contraceptive formulations, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not performed. CHCs do not protect against sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. If there is a risk of STI/HIV, correct and consistent use of condoms is recommended. Voluntary use of contraception is critical for upholding women’s reproductive rights. Women have the right to evidence-based, comprehensive contraceptive information, education, and counseling to ensure informed choice. Contraceptive choices are influenced by individual circumstances, societal and cultural contexts, and may change over time. Summary of Evidence: Evidence on whether CHC use affects fracture risk is inconsistent. Some studies show no effect, while others suggest a potential decrease in BMD in adolescents using very-low-dose CHCs. CHC use has little to no effect on BMD in premenopausal women and may preserve bone mass in perimenopausal women. The quality of evidence for fracture risk (direct) and BMD (indirect) is low to very low due to limitations, inconsistency, and indirectness in the studies reviewed. Quality of Evidence: For fracture risk, evidence is of low quality. For BMD in adolescents, evidence is of low quality for oral CHCs and very low quality for contraceptive patches. Conclusion: The use of CHCs is generally safe for most women, with specific considerations for age, cardiovascular risk, and bone health. Further research is needed to address gaps in evidence, particularly regarding the long-term effects of CHCs on bone health in adolescents and fracture risk in women of all ages.
